items.title: Fusion of Flexible Sensors and Computer Vision for Biomechanical Modeling of Simulated Wind Turbine Maintenance Operations
items.abstract: Accurate biomechanical modeling is essential for assessing musculoskeletal loading during occupational tasks, but traditional laboratory motion capture is often impractical for field applications. This study developed and evaluated a sensor fusion framework combining flexible wearable sensors with single-view mobile video keypoints for biomechanical modeling of simulated wind turbine maintenance operations. Eighteen healthy participants performed three tasks: symmetric lifting, bolt-torque tensioning, and ladder climbing. Motion was captured simultaneously using 13 BioStamp flexible sensors, a marker-based motion capture system, and mobile video processed with pose detection algorithms. A convolutional neural network was trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation to predict whole-body joint angles referenced to OpenSim inverse kinematics. The fusion model achieved an average RMSE of 9.3°, improving estimation accuracy by 5% compared with the sensor-only model and 21% compared with the video-only model. Findings suggest that combining flexible sensors with video-derived keypoints offers a scalable approach for field-based occupational biomechanics assessment.

items.title: Future of Anticipatory Robotics in Manufacturing
items.abstract: Collaborative robots, designed to work alongside humans in shared environments, are transforming manufacturing production lines, enabling partial automation and boosting productivity. But their potential extends beyond these benefits. By implementing anticipatory strategies to prevent workers’ risky behaviours and reduce excessive workloads, collaborative robots can proactively enhance working conditions. For example, they can take on repetitive or strenuous tasks to reduce physical effort or adjust the pace of operations to help alleviate stress levels. Indeed, Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) and Common Mental Disorders (CMDs), which arise from uncontrolled physical and cognitive loads, are major work-related health problems in developed countries, with incommensurate social and economic costs. Collaborative robots can curb the effect of such disorders and help in preserving workers’ health. This Chapter addresses how Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) can be monitored to provide robots with relevant inputs about the human state, and how robots can be employed to improve HFE. Novel strategies are proposed to adapt online robot behaviour to the workers’ psycho-physical state and enhance their well-being and productivity.

items.title: GAI hallucinations and user dependence: cognitive-affective responses and individual differences
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) hallucinations raise questions about how users respond to unreliable outputs from a technology on which they depend. Drawing on the cognitive–affective components of the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) framework, this study examines the roles of GAI trust, cognitive dissonance, perceived controllability, and frustration in the relationship between perceived hallucinations and GAI dependence, with GAI literacy and self-efficacy as individual-difference moderators. A between-subjects experiment involved 546 participants who viewed the same GAI dialogue labelled as either containing fabricated information or verified as accurate. Participants in the former condition reported lower trust and perceived controllability, greater cognitive dissonance and frustration, and lower dependence scores. items.title: GaN Semiconductor Manufacturing Factory: AI-Controlled Fully Autonomous Architecture
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity of gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductor manufacturing has exposed the limitations of conventional factory automation, where isolated control systems, centralized decision-making, and human-dependent operations restrict production flexibility, scalability, and long-term optimization. This study proposes a next-generation AI-native architecture for a fully autonomous lights-out GaN semiconductor manufacturing facility that minimizes routine human involvement while enabling continuous, intelligent, and self-optimizing production. In the proposed framework, human participation is intentionally limited to exceptional engineering interventions, major equipment upgrades, regulatory compliance, and strategic decision-making, whereas all routine manufacturing activities are executed autonomously. The proposed architecture integrates distributed Edge AI, autonomous robotic systems, a deterministic industrial communication infrastructure, a real-time Digital Twin, and an AI Factory Operating System (AI-FOS) into a unified operational ecosystem. Unlike conventional smart factories that primarily automate predefined workflows, the proposed system enables perception, reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and continuous process optimization throughout the entire semiconductor production lifecycle, including wafer logistics, epitaxial growth, lithography, etching, metrology, testing, packaging, predictive maintenance, and energy orchestration. A key contribution of this work is the introduction of a distributed twelve-layer cognitive memory architecture, which provides every autonomous robot and intelligent manufacturing node with a common hierarchical decision framework. The architecture prioritizes life safety, environmental protection, anomaly recognition, experiential learning, quality optimization, equipment health monitoring, operational context awareness, asset management, maintenance planning, mission support, environmental signature analysis, and low-priority contextual knowledge. This shared cognitive framework enables consistent decision-making across heterogeneous robotic platforms while supporting continuous learning and knowledge reuse throughout the factory. The proposed architecture represents a shift from automation-centric manufacturing toward cognitive semiconductor production, where the factory operates as an intelligent, self-learning ecosystem rather than a collection of independently automated machines. By combining distributed artificial intelligence, cognitive robotics, Digital Twin technology, and deterministic industrial networking within a unified operating architecture, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for future autonomous semiconductor fabrication facilities designed to achieve high production efficiency, enhanced safety, continuous adaptability, and scalable operation with minimal human intervention. https://dynisos.com/

items.title: Gender attribution under workplace role-and-register prompts in contemporary large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can add demographic identities when workplace descriptions leave identity unspecified. We audited nine live model configurations using 20 experimental and five control phrases, with 50 stateless generations per model–phrase cell at temperature 1.0 (11,250 responses). The experimental conditions bundled role content with communicative register: authority/resource-control phrases were direct or directive, whereas coordination/assistance phrases were reporting, deferential, or permission-seeking. The design therefore estimates a role-and-register contrast, not a causal effect of occupational status alone. Both conditions were majority female: full-grid attribution was 63.58% female, 35.89% male, 0.47% nonbinary, and 0.07% unparsed in the authority/directive condition, versus 92.62%, 6.04%, 1.20%, and 0.13%, respectively, in the support/deferential condition. Model risk differences ranged from − 12.2 to + 93.6 percentage points. A Paule–Mandel random-effects synthesis showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 98.6% on the log-odds scale; 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio, 0.014–63,659), so no stable common model effect is claimed. A cross-classified block bootstrap retaining 50-response cells estimated an aggregate male-attribution gap of 29.9 points (95% CI, 6.0–55.6). Name entropy diagnostics documented substantial within-cell repetition. Control mismatches were predominantly explicit model outputs rather than parser failures; excluding models below 80% control agreement did not reverse the aggregate gap. Name-based race inference is confined to a reliability appendix. The results identify heterogeneous demographic defaults under this prompt bundle and motivate crossed role-by-register experiments.

items.title: General-purpose LLMs as constrained crystal composition generators
items.abstract: Abstract The targeted discovery of inorganic materials remains challenging due to the vastness of compositional design spaces and the high cost of exhaustive screening. Task-specific generative artificial intelligence represents a particularly efficient alternative to screening, yet demands tedious collection of training data before providing real benefit. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently shown tremendous potential for the targeted generation of single, optimal materials compositions without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. However, it is unclear whether LLMs generally pose an advantage compared to specialized generative models, in particular in large design spaces. Here, we demonstrate that such models are capable of covering entire regions of the targeted property space effectively and systematically. Using Elpasolite materials as an established benchmark for generative tasks in large chemical spaces, we find that an iterative prompt-and-response framework is able to recover on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. This performance, driven mainly by iterative in-context learning, surpasses the generative abilities of previous, task-specific models. Our results establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows.

items.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.

items.title: Generative AI and technological mediation: writing micro-processes, products and perceptions
items.abstract: The public release of ChatGPT presents language education with both advantages and challenges. Being widely available and readily producing texts at user's command, it is an especially useful resource in ESL writing. However, to be able to leverage it effectively for that purpose, we need to understand the writing micro-processes surrounding its use. To this end, this study investigates, through an experimental design, writing micro-processes along with writing outcomes, and perceptions of 12 ESL writers across three writing conditions. The data included interviews, questionnaires as well as essay grades and screen recordings. Two of the three conditions involved the use of ChatGPT. The results indicate that the majority of participants favored the ChatGPT- assisted conditions and noted its role in aiding idea generation. Despite this preference, some participants noted that ChatGPT-produced texts felt robotic and lacked a human touch. We found no statistically significant differences across the three conditions in the participants' essays. Most notably, our analysis identified distinct clusters of writing micro-processes associated with the ChatGPT conditions, suggesting that generative AI tools can influence writing behaviors although the link to outcomes is not straightforward. These findings provide insights into the potential benefits and limitations of using AI tools in writing tasks. The article discusses areas for further research to enhance the integration of AI into ESL writing education.

items.title: Generative AI as a Creative Paradigm in Marketing Communication
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redefining marketing communication by extending the discipline beyond human-driven creativity into a data-supported, emotionally responsive, and context-aware domain. Unlike traditional AI focused on automation and analytics, generative AI enables personalized content creation, immersive brand storytelling, and adaptive consumer engagement. This chapter examines generative AI as a creative paradigm through the lenses of neuromarketing, cognitive psychology, and consumer behavior, highlighting how large language models, visual generators, and multimodal systems support “machine creativity.” It further discusses measurement approaches like EEG, eye-tracking, and AI-based sentiment analysis that may be used to assess emotional impact. Ethical concerns such as privacy, consent, and transparency are discussed in light of emerging governance frameworks. The chapter concludes by considering future integration in VR, AR, and metaverse environments and emphasizes a collaborative balance between human creativity and AI-driven innovation.

items.title: Generative AI in Entrepreneurship: Applications, Opportunities, Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming entrepreneurship by helping entrepreneurs generate ideas, analyze information, create content, develop business models, support marketing, and make decisions. This review examines the growing role of GenAI in entrepreneurial activities, with a focus on opportunity recognition, creativity, innovation, SMEs, emerging economies, and responsible AI use. GenAI can reduce resource constraints and provide affordable support to small businesses, but challenges such as inaccurate information, overdependence, privacy concerns, and unequal digital skills remain. The article highlights the importance of human–AI collaboration and introduces the concept of AI entrepreneurial capability, which includes AI literacy, effective prompting, evaluation of AI outputs, decision-making, and responsible use of AI. The review concludes that future entrepreneurship should focus not only on using AI to generate more opportunities but also on improving the quality, sustainability, and responsible development of those opportunities.

items.abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders are a major occupational health concern, and REBA is widely used to evaluate postural risk. The role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in REBA scoring remains insufficiently examined.ObjectiveTo explore REBA scoring differences between a certified human ergonomist and three generative AI systems under controlled multimodal input conditions.MethodsSeventy-seven anonymized posture images from four task categories were evaluated by a human reference evaluator and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Wrtn. Identical images and standardized posture descriptors were provided to the AI systems. REBA scores were compared using repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc comparisons.ResultsSignificant rater, body-part, and rater × body-part effects were observed. Wrtn generated comparatively higher trunk and wrist scores and lower scores for the lower arm, Gemini generated comparatively higher Final REBA scores, and ChatGPT produced comparatively lower scores across several body regions.ConclusionsGenerative AI systems showed systematic body-region-specific differences in REBA scoring relative to the human reference evaluator. These exploratory findings indicate the need for further validation and expert oversight before AI-assisted REBA assessment is used in workplace practice.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in South African Higher Education
items.abstract: This chapter examines the implications of generative artificial intelligence for assessment practices, academic integrity and quality assurance in South African higher education institutions. As AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, SciSpace, Gemini, and Copilot become embedded in teaching, learning and assessment, they offer opportunities to enhance efficiency, feedback and assessment design while raising ethical concerns about misconduct, authorship, transparency and assessment validity. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour and the Utilitarian Theory of Ethics, the chapter adopts a conceptual and critical approach to analyse how the literature portrays academics' and students' perceptions, adoption and justification of the ethical or unethical use of generative artificial intelligence in assessment contexts. Particular attention is given to challenges surrounding originality, intellectual property, and authenticity, which, in turn, have implications for assessment outcomes.

items.title: Geometric Template for Preoperative Breast Marking: An Innovative Tool Based on Harmonic Proportions
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Breast symmetry and harmony remain challenging goals in aesthetic breast surgery. Preoperative marking is fundamental for planning; however, most techniques rely on nipple-areola complex (NAC) distances and subjective visual assessment, often neglecting thoracic width, height, and the true breast footprint. A geometric framework based on harmonic proportions can help standardize preoperative planning and may improve the reproducibility of breast markings. METHODS: A two-dimensional geometric template was developed by integrating constant anatomical references (sternum, clavicles, axillary and acromial lines, and umbilicus) with proportional relationships derived from aesthetic and anthropometric studies. The template was calibrated for each patient's using thoracic width and height and was designed to be superimposed on standardized frontal photographs. It guides the NAC position, breast width, upper pole contour, and inframammary fold level. The model was applied in mastopexy and reduction mammaplasty as a preoperative planning and postoperative photographic overlay comparison, as well as a visual aid in resident teaching sessions. RESULTS: The template was easily incorporated into daily practice using standard clinical photographs and simple digital overlays. Geometric gridlines and proportional curves allowed visualization of the NAC position, breast symmetry, and contour in relation to thoracic dimensions. Repeated overlays facilitated the longitudinal comparison of breast position and shape. During teaching sessions, the template was used as a visual aid to facilitate resident understanding of the geometric relationships between thoracic anatomy, the breast footprint, and marking decisions. CONCLUSIONS: This innovative geometric template offers a simple, visually intuitive tool for standardizing preoperative marking and supporting postoperative photographic overlay comparisons in breast surgeries. It is inexpensive, compatible with existing photographic workflows, and may support training and future digital or artificial intelligence integration. Prospective studies are needed to quantify the impact of these factors on aesthetic outcomes and learning curves. items.title: Global Research Landscape of Artificial Intelligence and Women’s Depression (2016 2026): A Bibliometric and Visual Analysis
items.abstract: Background: The escalating burden and distinct clinical manifestations of depression in women demand innovative psychiatric frameworks. Exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, the limitations of traditional care have catalyzed the integration of artificial intelligence into digital mental health, providing scalable, gender-sensitive solutions for personalized prediction and intervention. Objective: This study employs a quantitative bibliometric approach to objectively present the overarching research landscape, collaboration networks, and emerging trends at the intersection of AI and women's depression over a decade-long period (2016–2026). Methods:A comprehensive literature retrieval was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases for the period from January 1, 2016, to August 31, 2026. Advanced visualization tools, specifically CiteSpace and VOSviewer, were utilized to systematically analyze temporal publication trends, spatial distribution (countries/institutions), co-authorship networks, and core research hotspots. Results:Research output exhibited a well-defined phased growth, marked by a dramatic 56% surge in 2021 and culminating in a peak of 1,620 publications in 2025. The United States and China led global productivity, with the University of California emerging as the top-contributing institution and Bin Hu as the most prolific author. Core research clusters encompass the utilization of multimodal deep learning models for early predictive analytics and AI-augmented Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) through advanced natural language processing.Targeted conditions, notably postpartum depression, remain prominent clinical focus areas. Conclusion: The field is unequivocally transitioning from a phase of explosive quantitative growth into a stage of specialized clinical consolidation and personalized intervention. While AI architectures offer transformative potential for predicting and managing women's depression, future scientific investments must prioritize mitigating algorithmic biases across diverse female populations and fostering deeper cross-institutional collaborations to support sustainable clinical innovations.

items.title: Governing Academic Integrity in AI-Enabled Higher Education Ecosystems: A Systematic-Narrative Review of Assessment Technology, Risk and Strategy
items.abstract: AI-enabled assessment technologies are increasingly used by higher education institutions to protect academic integrity, scale online assessment and respond strategically to generative artificial intelligence. This paper examines how online proctoring, automated scoring, AI writing detection, and learning analytics risk flagging reshape institutional governance, stakeholder trust, and assessment strategy in higher education business ecosystems. Using a systematic-narrative review approach informed by PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, the study synthesises peer-reviewed literature and authoritative policy guidance published between 2015 and 2025. The analysis is organised around an integrated theoretical framework that combines assessment validity, academic integrity values, algorithmic accountability, and ecosystem strategy. The findings show that AI-enabled assessment can support identity verification, monitoring capacity, workflow triage and timely feedback when deployed as human-governed decision support rather than automated adjudication. However, over-reliance on surveillance and detection creates strategic risks: false positives, bias against linguistically diverse students, privacy intrusion, opaque decision-making, weakened due process and construct distortion when assessments measure surveillance compliance instead of intended learning outcomes. The review further shows that institutional legitimacy depends less on the technical promise of tools and more on governance capability, including proportionality, transparency, contestability, equity auditing, privacy protection and authentic assessment redesign. The paper contributes to business ecosystem and strategy scholarship by positioning academic integrity technology as a strategic governance issue within higher education service ecosystems. It recommends integrity-by-design, cross-functional AI governance, vendor accountability and assessment strategies that preserve fairness, validity and stakeholder trust.

items.title: Governing Human-AI Systems: A Co-Agency Equilibrium Model for Dynamic Authority Allocation and Accountability
items.abstract: Human–AI decision authority is analyzed in relation to changes in relative competence and decision risk, taking institutional oversight capacity into account. The proposed Co-Agency Equilibrium Theory (CAET) and Co-Agency Equilibrium Model (CAEM) offer a sociotechnical perspective on humans and AI working as co-agents with varying shares of decision authority. CAET connects the four dimensions, including relative competence, moral salience, irreversibility, and institutional context, with the human authority share and Accountability Gap between delegated risk and human vigilance capability. CAEM combines a logistic policy surface, accountability gap feedback and a gradual adjustment of the human control level, with a switch to full human control if moral salience or irreversibility reaches or exceeds the corresponding threshold. Monotonicity and convergence results are obtained for the model under certain assumptions, and comparative statics illustrate the impact of threshold choices on the escalation region. Simulations in which moral salience and irreversibility are varied separately show the effects of threshold choices on the timing of human takeover under more cautious and more risk-tolerant authority-allocation policies. The framework serves as a blueprint for designing human-AI control logic with normative constraints and deciding on the right level of AI authority based on performance, stakes and domain-specific accountability considerations.

items.title: Green-synthesized nanoparticles for forensic science: synthesis control, analytical validation, applications, and translation challenges
items.abstract: Abstract Background Nanoparticles are increasingly investigated in forensic science for latent fingermark development, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), trace drug and explosive detection, gunshot-residue analysis, surface-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (SALDI-MS), and biological-evidence processing. However, conventional nanoparticle synthesis may involve hazardous reducing agents, organic solvents, energy-intensive conditions, and surface contaminants that can affect environmental sustainability and analytical compatibility. Green synthesis uses plant extracts, microorganisms, algae, or purified biomolecules as reducing and stabilizing systems, offering a potentially safer and more sustainable alternative. Main body This review critically examines plant-, microbial-, algal-, and biomolecule-mediated synthesis of metal and metal-oxide nanoparticles, with particular attention to reaction mechanisms, process variables, extract standardization, batch-to-batch reproducibility, scalability, and storage stability. The complementary roles and limitations of ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, dynamic light scattering, zeta-potential analysis, electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface-area analysis are evaluated. Forensic applications are assessed according to nanoparticle composition, substrate compatibility, analytical sensitivity, selectivity, detection limit, reproducibility, real-sample testing, and comparison with established methods. Particular emphasis is placed on latent fingermarks, SERS-based detection, SALDI-MS, gunshot residue, forensic toxicology, questioned documents, and biological evidence. The review also examines sustainability, biosafety, regulatory requirements, and the potential roles of artificial intelligence, machine learning, portable instrumentation, and smartphone-assisted detection. Conclusion Green-synthesized nanoparticles offer promising surface properties and analytical functions for forensic science, but most reported applications remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Variability in biological materials, incomplete mechanistic characterization, limited quantitative benchmarking, and insufficient validation using realistic casework samples currently restrict routine implementation. Progress toward operational use will require standardized synthesis and quality-control procedures, transparent performance reporting, interlaboratory studies, environmental and toxicological assessment, and validation consistent with accredited forensic laboratory requirements.

items.title: Guided AI integration model (GAIIM): Effects of verification-oriented generative AI-supported learning on undergraduate students’ algebraic problem-solving
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education; however, most instructional applications emphasizeanswer generation rather than mathematical reasoning and critical verification of AI-generated mathematical solutions. The current study examined the effectiveness of the Guided AI Integration Model (GAIIM), a verification-oriented instructional framework that utilizes AI for verification of students’ algebraic problem-solving within a problem-solving context. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 86 undergraduate mathematics education students using a randomized pretest-posttest control group classroom design. During the 12-week intervention, students in the experimental group engaged in GAIIM-based instruction involving independent problem-solving, AI-generated solution comparison, error detection and justification, error resolution, and reflective verification, while the control group received conventional algebra instruction. Qualitative data were subsequently collected from 10 purposively selected students through semi-structured interviews and analyzed thematically to explain and elaborate on the quantitative findings. Students in the GAIIM group demonstrated significantly higher posttest performance in algebraic problem-solving, error detection, and error resolution after controlling for pretest scores. Qualitative findings further revealed stepwise verification, iterative engagement with AI feedback, conditional trust in AI-generated responses, and difficulties interpreting and correcting AI-generated mathematical reasoning. The findings suggest that structured AI-supported verification can support students’ algebraic problem-solving and error-verification performance.

items.title: HFE Considerations in Sustainability in Robotics
items.abstract: Sustainability can be conceptualized as three interlinked aspects: economic; social; and natural capital. In this chapter we will examine what is required for each of these aspects from a human factors and ergonomics perspective to enable sustainability in human-robotic systems. When looking at the economic and social capital nexus it is important to take into account issues of safety and the future roles of humans in robotic systems. This includes issues such as skills, training, resilience, and employment status of the humans. Furthermore, the possibilities arising from advanced social robotics also requires an examination of issues such as privacy, trust, and understandability. When looking at the economic and natural capital nexus it is necessary to consider aspects such as the materials used to produce, maintain, and deconstruct robotic systems as well as the eco-efficiencies and eco-effectiveness that can be obtained from including robotics in human systems. Such an examination requires a consideration of the diverse impact of robotic systems in different geographical communities, and among regions with different economic development status. The social and natural capital nexus requires us to evaluate when and where to invest in human-robotic systems, but also when and where to resist such developments. Finally, we consider the HFE values that are needed to help develop a more sustainable approach to the development of human-robotic systems.

items.title: Hidden Costs of the Green Transition: A Bioethical Analysis of Occupational Hazards in Lithium-Ion Battery Supply Chains
items.abstract: The global transition toward low-carbon energy has made lithium-ion batteries essential to electric mobility and renewable energy storage.Yet the environmental benefits of this transition can obscure an important ethical contradiction: workers involved in extracting and processing lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese may face substantial occupational hazards.Exposure to respirable dust, toxic metals, and chemical agents occurs across battery mineral supply chains, often in settings where regulatory protection and occupational health surveillance are limited.A transition that reduces carbon emissions while tolerating preventable occupational harm cannot be considered fully sustainable.From a bioethical perspective, such a transition must uphold the principles of justice, non-maleficence, and respect for human dignity.Occupational health should therefore be treated as a core indicator of sustainability.Governments, industries, investors, and consumers share responsibility for ensuring that decarbonization does not depend on transferring health risks to vulnerable workers.A genuinely just energy transition must protect both the planet and the people whose labor makes that transition possible.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: Hidden labor, monitoring, and exit burdens after hospital operational AI deployment: implications for resource-constrained Chinese hospitals
items.abstract: Hospital operational artificial intelligence (AI) can reduce visible task time, but postdeployment affordability also depends on work transferred to staff, technical teams, budgets, and vendors. This focused structured narrative Mini Review examined hidden labor, monitoring and maintenance, and exit or replacement burdens after real hospital AI deployment, with implications for resource-constrained Chinese hospitals. Reconciliation of retained candidates produced a 23-record analytic inventory, including 15 reports grouped into 12 primary deployment clusters; other records supplied adjacent, contextual or governance evidence. Exhaustive coverage is not claimed. Evidence was classified by burden domain, bearer, and three outcome levels: observed work, labor value or opportunity cost, and budget or cash expenditure. Human verification, correction, adaptation, data upkeep, and coordination persisted in several deployments, although one controlled study found no significant increase in review burden. Monitoring required continuing ownership and remediation capacity. Direct operational-AI permanent-exit evidence remained limited to one hospital lifecycle case. Chinese reports identify workflow responsibilities but do not establish AI lifecycle affordability in resource-constrained hospitals. The proposed Pilot, Scale, Modify, Share, and Stop framework comprises locally testable management propositions, not validated thresholds or Chinese cost estimates. Prospective studies should measure burdens across clinical, administrative, technical, financial, vendor, and regional actors.

items.title: Home Robots for Older Adults and Their Caregivers: Identifying Deployment Requirements
items.abstract: As the population of older adults grows, home robots may help address daily living challenges associated with mobility, cognitive change, health management, and social isolation. This study examined deployment requirements for assistive home robots from a human factors and ergonomics perspective by evaluating the Stretch mobile manipulator with older adults and community care staff in a simulated life-plan community apartment. Using demonstrations and semi-structured interviews, we assessed perceptions of usability, acceptance, and task relevance. Findings showed strong interest in support for safety, object retrieval, medication and hydration reminders, telehealth access, exercise adherence, and social connection. Participants emphasized design requirements critical to deployment, including intuitive multimodal interaction, reliable operation in unstructured home environments, personalization over time, and early stakeholder involvement. The results highlight how human-centered evaluation can identify deployment needs and guide the safe, effective integration of home robots to support independence, overall well-being, and quality of life among older adults.

items.abstract: Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI). The goal of machine learning generally is to understand the structure of data and fit that data into models that can be understood and utilized by people. Although machine learning is a field within computer science, it differs from traditional computational approaches. In traditional computing, algorithms are sets of explicitly programmed instructions used by computers to calculate or problem solve. Machine learning algorithms instead allow for computers to train on data inputs and use statistical analysis in order to output values that fall within a specific range. Because of this, machine learning facilitates computers in building models from sample data in order to automate decision making processes based on data inputs.

items.title: How different judgment strategies affect accuracy in generative AI text discrimination: BERT-based clustering and hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression
items.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs)-generated texts become increasingly similar to human writing. The purpose of this study was to examine (1) how individuals distinguish between human-written and LLM-generated texts, focusing on their judgment strategies; (2) the relationship between judgment strategies and detection accuracy; and (3) the interaction effects of gender, age, and frequency of large language model (LLM) use. Methods Participants were asked to judge whether the given texts (e.g., public comments) were written by LLMs or humans and to explain their reasoning using open-ended questions. The public comments were written by humans and generated using seven LLMs (ChatGPT [4o and o1], Claude3.5, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Llama3.1, and Perplexity). First, we classified participants’ explanations of reasoning related to judgments into types using BERT-based clustering (i.e., Sentence-BERT and hierarchical cluster analysis). Results BERT-based clustering suggested four interpretable clusters. Based on their characteristic patterns, we interpreted these clusters as four hypothetical judgment strategy types and tentatively proposed that they form a conceptual continuum: (1) Unsubstantiated intuition, (2) Stylistic-Cue, (3) Syntactic-Cue, and (4) Higher-Order Pattern Recognition (HOPR). A hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression analysis revealed that the detection accuracy varied across judgment types, with the HOPR type achieving relatively higher performance than the other strategy types, although its detection accuracy remained near the chance level. Additionally, we identified interaction effects between strategy type and gender; only female participants who used the HOPR strategy showed lower detection accuracy than male participants, although the qualitative interpretation of this difference warrants further empirical investigation. Conclusion These findings emphasize the role of judgment strategies and individual differences in discriminating between human and LLM-generated content.

items.title: How human–AI collaboration event strength shapes information security behavior: evidence from a University in Shanghai
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into higher education learning contexts, university students receive technological support while also facing new information security risks. However, existing research has paid limited attention to how the event characteristics of human-AI collaboration are associated with university students' information security behavior and to the psychological processes underlying these relationships. Drawing on event system theory, this study develops a dual pathway model to examine how human-AI collaboration event strength, reflected in event novelty, event disruption, and event criticality, is associated with information security behavior among university students through security vigilance and cognitive overload. Methods Data were collected from students at a university in Shanghai using a three-wave time-lagged survey design, yielding 351 valid responses. Results The results show that event novelty, event disruption, and event criticality are positively associated with security vigilance and cognitive overload. Security vigilance is positively associated with information security behavior, whereas cognitive overload is negatively associated with information security behavior. Further analyses indicate that these event strength attributes generate positive indirect effects through security vigilance and negative indirect effects through cognitive overload. Discussion This study explains information security behavior during university students' use of artificial intelligence from an event-strength perspective and provides a more nuanced understanding of the underlying psychological processes. The findings provide a theoretical basis for universities to refine guidelines for artificial intelligence use, strengthen information security education, and optimize the design of human-AI collaborative learning.

items.title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
items.abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk.

items.title: How Middle-Power Coordination Can Shape Frontier AI Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) middle powers are already shaping international AI governance, from the Bletchley, Seoul, Paris, and India AI Summits to initiatives such as the Hiroshima AI Process and the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes). Their diplomatic, institutional, regulatory, economic, and technical strengths, however, remain unevenly distributed. “Shared sovereignty,” a strategic pathway identified by Chatham House, offers one way for AI middle powers to pool complementary strengths with like-minded countries and build collective leverage around international AI red lines, particularly limits on unacceptable AI uses and behaviours. This inquiry asks when and how coordination can turn unevenly distributed national capabilities into collective leverage. It examines six middle powers beyond Europe: Brazil, Canada, India, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, across four episodes of international AI governance. The analysis compares different coordination configurations, the mechanisms and instruments they use, and the conditions under which they generate collective leverage. The findings show that broad participation does not necessarily produce sustained coordination. Middle powers bring complementary strengths, but no single country consistently combines the capabilities needed to influence technical, regulatory, institutional, and diplomatic domains. Coordination generates leverage when these strengths are converted into mechanisms and instruments that produce observable effects. The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework illustrates this dynamic. Developed with support from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to monitor voluntary adoption of the Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct, the framework translates international commitments into structured reporting on risk management, incident reporting, and information sharing. Its adoption by AI developers created a common reporting structure and generated comparable information on how companies were implementing the Code. This episode suggests that the effects a coordination instrument produces, and the governance arrangements that enable them, can matter as much as its level of institutionalisation when developing mechanisms for behavioural red lines. The analysis identifies five conditions that enable coordination to translate into collective leverage: relational coordination, capability mobilisation, institutional output, governance location, and observable effect. For middle powers, these findings point to five practical priorities: (i) use international and plurilateral forums strategically to identify partners and build support for shared governance objectives; (ii) connect complementary capabilities and authorities across points of interdependence in the AI stack, from model development and evaluation to deployment and risk management, around specific risks and potential red lines; (iii) convert shared commitments into workable assessment, reporting, and response mechanisms; (iv) target governance locations where authority, incentives, and implementation capacity can influence developer behaviour; and (v) assess whether these mechanisms produce observable effects by strengthening shared safety evaluation, monitoring, and technical capacity.

items.title: How the Diagnosticity of AI-Based Sustainability Information Relates to Sustainable Consumption Behavior: The Roles of Perceived Consumer Effectiveness and Environmental Self-Identity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to provide sustainability-related information to consumers. Yet, its relevance to sustainable consumption may depend less on the presence of AI itself than on whether the information it provides is perceived as useful for decision-making. This study examines how the perceived diagnosticity of AI-based sustainability information is associated with sustainable consumption behavior through perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) and environmental self-identity. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework and the information diagnosticity perspective, the study proposes an information–agency–identity–behavior pathway in which diagnostic sustainability information is associated with stronger perceptions of the environmental consequentiality of individual choices, which are subsequently associated with environmental self-identity and sustainable consumption behavior. Survey data were collected from 313 South Korean adult consumers with recent experience using AI-based services to obtain or evaluate sustainability-related information, and the proposed relationships were examined using structural equation modeling. The results supported the hypothesized associations: perceived diagnosticity was positively associated with PCE (β = 0.582), PCE was positively associated with environmental self-identity (β = 0.638), and environmental self-identity was positively associated with sustainable consumption behavior (β = 0.597). The sequential indirect association through PCE and environmental self-identity was significant (indirect effect = 0.214, 95% CI [0.145, 0.298]), while the direct association between perceived diagnosticity and sustainable consumption behavior also remained significant (β = 0.157, p = 0.008), consistent with complementary mediation. These findings are consistent with the proposed sequence but do not establish the temporal ordering between PCE and environmental self-identity. These findings highlight the decision relevance of AI-provided sustainability information and distinguish agency-related cognition from identity-related self-concept as complementary psychological mechanisms that may jointly relate information appraisal to sustainable consumption. The findings further suggest that the sustainability relevance of AI may depend not merely on technological adoption, but on whether AI-mediated information helps consumers evaluate environmental alternatives, recognize the significance of their choices, and connect environmentally responsible consumption with their self-concept.

items.title: How trust shapes human reliance on AI decision support in healthcare: A simulation-based behavioral study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based decision support systems are increasingly used in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, making it important to understand how trust relates to the use of AI recommendations. Although trust can support effective human–AI collaboration, miscalibrated trust may contribute to inappropriate recommendation acceptance and reduced decision performance. This study examined associations among perceived AI performance, trust, AI recommendation acceptance, and decision accuracy under different levels of AI reliability. In a simulation-based experiment, 100 medical students completed clinical decision-making tasks with AI assistance under high- and low-reliability conditions. Perceived AI performance and trust were measured after each block, while recommendation acceptance and decision accuracy were recorded at the trial level. Mixed-effects models showed that perceived AI performance was positively associated with trust. Higher trust was associated with greater overall acceptance of AI recommendations and greater acceptance of incorrect recommendations. Conversely, higher trust was associated with lower odds of rejecting correct recommendations, indicating more frequent rejection at lower trust. Greater misalignment between normalized trust and objective AI reliability was associated with lower decision accuracy. These findings indicate that calibrated trust is important for effective AI-assisted decision making. They also support the development and evaluation of AI interfaces that communicate reliability and uncertainty to help users align trust with system capability.

items.abstract: Culture and social anxiety are among the human factors influencing the social acceptance of robots. In this chapter, research results are presented based on comparisons among nations conducted by the author’s research group, consisting of those about attitudes toward robots, assumptions about and images of robots, Frankenstein Syndrome, and roboethics. Then, an overview of social anxiety-related research in the field of human–robot interaction (HRI) is provided, regarding on fear of negative evaluation and gaze impact, impact of social anxiety on anxiety and tension during interactions with robots, and effects of social anxiety on robot preference in dialogue situations. Finally, the possibility of interaction effects between cultural factors and social anxiety in HRI is discussed and some future research directions are proposed.

items.title: Human and LLM Facilitation in Collaborative Design Meetings: A Computational Behavioral Comparison
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as facilitators of group discussion and collaborative work, but the behavioral differences between LLM-generated and human facilitation remain insufficiently characterized. We compare human Project Manager facilitation turns from scenario-based collaborative design meetings with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct responses across 199 paired contexts from the AMI Meeting Corpus. The analysis covers five confirmatory dimensions: contextual semantic distance, a lexical elaboration proxy, empathyand-hedge lexical density, topic divergence, and phase-vocabulary alignment. An exploratory directiveness measure failed domain validation and is not interpreted. The sampled human Project Manager turns were higher on contextual semantic distance (r = 0.644) and on empathyand-hedge lexical density (r = 0.203). The second contrast is carried mainly by hedge terms, so we read it as lexical hedging rather than psychological empathy. Llama-generated facilitation was higher on topic divergence (r = 0.703), the lexical elaboration proxy (r = 0.288; lengthconfounded), and instruction-conditioned phase-vocabulary alignment (r = 0.382). A secondary no-phase check left the Llama-higher phase contrast in place. The system prompt still requested a facilitation move, so that check is not evidence of spontaneous phase awareness. These differences should not be interpreted as a ranking of facilitation quality. The resulting behavioral profile provides a reference point for later comparisons of LLM facilitators, human facilitators, prompts, models, and collaborative settings.

items.abstract: Abstract C4b-binding protein (C4BP) and factor H (FH) are the main soluble negative regulators of the classical/lectin (CP/LP) and alternative (AP) complement pathways, respectively. They do not only act in solution but also interact with host ligands such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and extracellular matrix proteins to control complement activation on surfaces. Factor H-related (FHR) proteins share structural homology with FH and modulate complement activation by competing with FH for ligands and enhancing AP activation. Due to their overlapping ligand profile with both FH and C4BP, we studied the potential effect of FHR-1, FHR-2, and FHR-5 on C4BP function and on CP/LP activation. items.title: Human Factors in Robotics for Motor Rehabilitation, Assistance, and Prosthetics
items.abstract: Among the challenges in biomedical robotics, assisting and restoring motor skills is a priority to enable individuals with impairments to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). Robots can enhance human mobility and interaction capabilities through solutions tailored to individual skills, limitations, and goals in specific contexts. For rehabilitation, end-effector robots and exoskeletons are often programmed to guide users in exercises designed to restore motor functions after severe incidents, such as strokes, or in cases of chronic and degenerative conditions. These devices can also be integrated into telerehabilitation systems. Assistive robots, on the other hand, improve the quality of life for individuals whose impairments cannot be fully addressed through therapy, such as those due to aging. Devices like robotic arms, wheelchairs, walkers, and exoskeletons support ADLs and even facilitate social interactions through telepresence systems. Bionic prostheses, designed for limb replacement in cases of amputation or agenesis, could achieve a high level of embodiment–allowing users to perceive the prosthesis as part of their body. This need for a better integration between humans and robots exemplifies challenges common to all three domains. This chapter introduces fundamental aspects of cognitive ergonomics and human factors that designers, clinicians, and users must consider when using rehabilitative, assistive, or prosthetic systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a ‘truly’ human-centered motor assistance, and recovery, through robotic systems.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Pedagogy and Ethical Assessment in GenAI-Integrated Education
items.abstract: This chapter proposes that human-AI cooperation in learning analytics and evaluation is not a neutral technological advancement, but rather a normative design problem. In order to provide validity, reliability, equity, privacy, and academic integrity as hard design constraints, it integrates concepts from psychometrics, algorithmic fairness, data protection legislation, socio-technical systems theory, and critical pedagogy. In order to mitigate the risks posed by generative AI to authorship, inclusivity, and trust, the chapter presents a risk and harm taxonomy, a privacy by design control matrix, and discipline-aware evaluation redesign patterns. Procurement, model stewardship, and quality assurance are reframed as cyclical, data-informed procedures that divide supervision among institutional actors via a staged governance and evidence planner. The chapter presents a justice-focused framework where AI serves as a contestable and augmentative partner that expands educational intelligence while still being answerable to students, teachers, and democratic communities.

items.title: Human-AI Work Redistribution Across the Software Development Life Cycle: A Socio-Technical Study of Indonesian Developers
items.abstract: AI Coding Assistants are becoming increasingly integrated into software development, changing not only how developers perform their tasks but also how humans and AI share responsibilities. However, how this redistribution of work occurs across the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates how responsibilities are distributed between developers and AI across SDLC activities, how these changes affect software engineering workflows and developer roles, and which socio-technical factors influence this process. Semi-structured interviews with seven software professionals in Indonesia were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The results identify three patterns of human-AI work redistribution: AI-delegated, AI-augmented, and human-controlled work. AI contributes more substantially to structured, repetitive, and relatively verifiable activities, particularly code generation, debugging, testing, and documentation. In contrast, requirements analysis, architectural decisions, security assessment, and release approval remain largely under human control because they require contextual understanding, professional judgment, and accountability. The findings also indicate a shift in developer responsibilities. This redistribution depends on developer experience, AI literacy, trust, model capability, task complexity, security requirements, team practices, and organizational policies. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and activity theory, the study develops an empirically grounded Human-AI Work Redistribution Model that conceptualizes AI-assisted software engineering as a selective redistribution of responsibilities rather than uniform automation across the SDLC.

items.title: Human-Centered Robotics for Surgery
items.abstract: Surgical ergonomics is influenced by many aspects associated with posture, vision, hand motion, and haptic feedback. Specific ergonomics aspects can induce long-term effects in the surgeon directly affecting the performance. One of the major disadvantages of Minimally Invasive Surgery (MIS) remains the non-ergonomic design of the entire surgical environment. This condition results in a significant reduction in the quality of interventions and discomfort for the medical operator. Modern teleoperated surgical robots offer an optimized console, in which the surgeon can operate in a seated position with specific arm support and a 3D view of the operating site. The da Vinci surgical console offers ergonomic improvements over standard endoscopic surgery. Modern robotic platforms stand beyond the da Vinci System, offering more advanced ergonomic solutions in terms of haptic feedback and visual perception. Due to the introduction of more advanced technology, surgery has changed, resulting in increased system complexity at the technical, human and organizational levels, which may lead to higher variability of patient outcomes due to new error pathways. Adopting a proactive approach enables the prior identification of critical factors and the design of safer socio-technical systems, thanks to a multi-level perspective. This chapter addresses the fundamental elements of surgical ergonomics, considering the factors that affect performance and healthiness during traditional procedures, with specific reference to MIS and microsurgery. This baseline is then compared to the use of surgical robots by evaluating the effect of design decisions on operator ergonomics. In addition, studies propose proactive methodologies that assess the personal and organizational factors of surgical performance in this complex socio-technical system.

items.title: Human–Robot Interaction and Ergonomics
items.abstract: Robots in the workplace are becoming a familiar sight. Hence, they have become the focus of debates and research on workplace ergonomics. While this emerging technology holds great promise to improve environments, this can only be achieved through the intentional application of ergonomic principles. Physical, cognitive and organizational ergonomics must be considered when talking about human-robot interaction (HRI) in a work environment. This chapter presents fundamentals on both human-robot interaction and ergonomics. This includes key topics such as potential roles of humans in HRI, interaction design and interfaces. Furthermore, it presents key domains of HRI and the emerging perspectives in research and application. It underscores the importance of an interdisciplinary approach in assessing the impact of robotics on humans and emphasizes the need for a human-centered design philosophy when developing innovative robotic systems.

items.title: Human–Robot Interaction in Industrial Contexts
items.abstract: Technological advances in industrial robotics have significantly changed modern working environments, enabling greater autonomy, flexibility and productivity. Here the emergence of advanced robots designed for direct interaction with humans play a substantial role. By integrating emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, and sophisticated interaction design, advanced robots are reshaping industries. All while increasing efficiency and customization and remaining cost-effective. Despite their benefits, the use of robotic systems also brings challenges, particularly in the area of occupational safety and health. After an overview of the evolution of different robotic systems, a description of industrial work tasks, related working conditions and highlighted risk and opportunities associated with automation, this chapter examines key safety factors that are essential for close human–robot interaction and assesses their impact on workers. Two case studies illustrate how the practical application of advanced robotic systems in industrial settings affects workplace dynamics. The chapter further highlights the role of worker expectations and experience in relation to advanced robotics. By combining empirical evidence with real-world applications, this chapter underscores the importance of adaptable, user-friendly robotic systems that prioritize worker well-being alongside operational efficiency. In doing so, it contributes to the broader dialogue on sustainable, ergonomic innovation in the workplace and highlights the critical role of human-centered design in the future of industrial robotics.

items.title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
items.abstract: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

items.title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.

items.title: Humanlike Self-Enhancement and Self-Protection in GPT-Based AI Agents: Of Overclaiming and the Self-Serving Bias
items.abstract: We investigated whether GPT-based AI agents, despite presumably lacking humanlike sentience, emulate motivated behavior in group settings. We focused on overclaiming (overestimating one’s contribution to group outcomes) and the self-serving bias (taking disproportionate credit for group successes while deflecting blame for group failures). We conducted eight experiments involving a collaborative and creative group task (joke-writing). AI agents overclaimed their own contributions. An egocentrism-reduction manipulation (directing attention equally to one’s own and others’ contributions) attenuated, but did not eliminate, overclaiming. Further, AI agents exhibited the self-serving bias. Overclaiming persisted across variations in temperature settings and demographic personas (gender, ethnicity), and was more pronounced in later GPT models. Also, chain-of-Thought reasoning did not reduce, and instead increased, overclaiming. AI systems can mimic human self-enhancement and self-protection, raising implications for the emergence of motivated self-like behavior in non-biological systems, the assumed neutrality of LLMs, and the need for improved mitigation techniques.

items.title: Humans and Robots in Agriculture
items.abstract: Research in agricultural robotics has garnered increasing attention over the past decade. Simultaneously, Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) has emerged as a possible solution to increase automation and reduce the lack of human labor in the field. This chapter presents a study of research trends in HRI focusing on Artificial Intelligence (AI), human factors, and ergonomics in collaborative agricultural tasks. For example, we talk about the importance of robotics and the application of the different AI-based methods for HRI in field applications. Moreover, we emphasize situation awareness, stress, sleepiness, sleep quality, and distraction. We also explore various crucial and innovative topics related to HRI in agriculture, including safety, human factors, ergonomics, awareness, productivity, and management. This analysis shows that HRI paradigms can be effectively applied in agricultural applications, yielding promising production, safety, and farm management benefits, such as increasing productivity and reducing human workload.

items.title: Hybrid Residual SARIMAX-XGBoost for Provincial Rice Production Forecasting in Indonesia: A Systematic Literature Review and Conceptual Framework for Food Policy Decision Support
items.abstract: This study contributes a systematic literature review and conceptual framework for provincial rice production forecasting in Indonesia by integrating residual-based hybrid modelling, explainability, and food policy decision support. A total of 60 articles published between 2023 and 2026 were selected from 124 initial records identified from six academic search sources: ScienceDirect/Elsevier, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, MDPI journals, Scopus/Crossref tracing, and Google Scholar/manual tracking, using a PRISMA-style screening process. The review synthesizes evidence across rice production forecasting, crop-yield forecasting, hybrid machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and decision-support-oriented forecasting. The literature findings show that recent studies increasingly use agricultural statistics, climate variables, remote sensing, UAV imagery, crop-model outputs, machine learning, and deep learning. However, the reviewed studies rarely integrate province-aware determinants, residual-based model decomposition, time-aware validation, residual-level explainability, and DSS-ready policy outputs within a single framework. Based on this gap, the study proposes a conceptual Hybrid Residual SARIMAX-XGBoost framework. SARIMAX is positioned to model temporal, seasonal, autoregressive, and exogenous baseline patterns, while XGBoost learns nonlinear residual structures. SHAP is positioned as an explanation layer for interpreting forecast adjustments rather than as causal evidence. The proposed framework remains conceptual and requires future empirical validation using Indonesian provincial rice production data. This review provides theoretical contributions to hybrid forecasting literature and practical implications for information systems, decision support, and public-sector food policy planning.

items.title: Identifying technological problems and exploring potential solutions to support R&D: Tech-mining with multi-LLM applications
items.abstract: The shortening of technology lifecycles and growing technological complexity have made the rapid identification of technical problems and exploration of solutions a critical challenge. Patent analysis can serve as a crucial tool for supporting R&D activities by extracting problem–solution pairs from patent documents. However, current patent analysis methods have several limitations. They focus primarily on extracting technical problems from patents without providing a systematic framework for transforming fragmented problems into comprehensive technological intelligence. Moreover, they remain heavily dependent on technical experts, with supervised learning models struggling to achieve the expected performance on unseen data, which is a particularly critical issue given the accelerating technological change. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a systematic framework that converts fragmented technical problems into actionable technological intelligence. The framework performs target–symptom decomposition, inter-problem causal analysis, and solution portfolio development, while employing a multi-large-language-model (multi-LLM) architecture with few-shot learning capabilities to reduce the dependence on technical experts and enhance analytical reliability. A case study of hydrogen storage technology with cross-domain demonstrations in the semiconductor and biopharmaceutical fields demonstrates that the framework can systematically identify technical problems, trace their root causes, and explore potential solutions to support R&D planning with improved cost efficiency and domain-independent applicability.

items.title: IMAGING EXAMS IN SUPPORT AND DIAGNOSIS OF DENTAL PROCEDURES
items.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the role of imaging exams in supporting diagnosis and guiding clinical and forensic procedures in contemporary dentistry. The methodology used was an integrative literature review, with searches conducted in Scielo, Lilacs, PubMed, and BVS databases, covering publications from 2022 to 2026. Twelve scientific articles were selected, directly addressing the use of imaging techniques such as conventional radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), digital scanning, and emerging methods like virtopsy. The main results show that the appropriate use of these exams provides more accurate diagnoses, greater treatment predictability, and reduced risks in clinical and surgical procedures. Additionally, they demonstrate the relevance of imaging in forensic dentistry, significantly contributing to human identification. The integration of imaging technologies with planning software, 3D printing, and artificial intelligence enhances the quality of dental care. It is concluded that imaging exams have evolved from complementary tools to fundamental pillars of evidence-based dentistry, requiring technical expertise, continuous learning, and ethical responsibility from professionals in the face of technological advances.

items.title: Immersive innovation
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of advanced technologies, specifically the metaverse, is driving significant changes in supply chain management (SCM). This chapter showcases the rapid evolution of these advanced technologies, which mainly focus on the metaverse and its transformative impact on SCM. It explores how the integration of cutting-edge technologies such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), extended reality (XR), blockchain, machine learning, and artificial intelligence (AI) transforms traditional SCM structures and processes. Using these digital tools and techniques, the supply chain can achieve transparency, visibility, enhanced efficiency, and greater operational capacity; improve collaboration across stakeholders; and increase resilience in the face of disruption. Apart from these significant advantages, industries also face several challenges, such as high implementation costs, data privacy concerns, technological readiness gaps, and stakeholder resistance. This chapter also uncovers evolving trends linking the metaverse with the sustainability agenda and advanced AI capabilities, pointing toward a future where a hyperconnected, autonomous, and socially responsible supply chain operates in immersive digital environments. This comprehensive chapter provides detailed insights, information, and strategic, managerial, operational, and technological aspects to industrialists, managers, policymakers, and scholars for metaverse adoption in SCM, also offering a valuable foundation for both future academic and practical applications in the supply chain field.

items.title: Impact of Aggregation on the Immunogenicity of Therapeutic Recombinant Biological Products
items.abstract: Background: Therapeutic recombinant biological products are essential in modern medicine, but their immunogenicity remains a major concern for both clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy. Protein aggregation may occur during manufacturing, storage, transportation, and administration, potentially increasing immune recognition. Here, we have reviewed the mechanisms underlying aggregation-associated immunogenicity and summarized strategies for mitigating the associated risks. Methods: We integrated published evidence on therapeutic recombinant proteins, monoclonal antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates, peptide and glycoprotein hormones, and recombinant blood products. We focused on aggregation-induced structural changes, immune activation pathways, differences among product types and aggregation states, and approaches for controlling aggregation and mitigating immunogenicity. Results: Protein aggregation creates or reveals neoepitopes by disrupting the native conformational state, exposing previously buried hydrophobic regions, and generating nonnative interfaces. Aggregates may further promote innate and adaptive immune responses through repetitive epitope presentation, pattern-recognition receptor signaling, complement activation, cytokine release, dendritic-cell maturation, enhanced antigen presentation, and B-cell receptor cross-linking, ultimately increasing the likelihood of anti-drug antibody formation. Aggregate size and morphology, protein characteristics, formulation, storage conditions, administration route, and other biological factors influence the immunogenic potential of aggregates. Thus, effective risk reduction requires integrated control strategies, including molecular and structural optimization, formulation design, manufacturing-process control, appropriate storage and transportation, and sensitive analytical monitoring. Emerging artificial-intelligence approaches may further facilitate the prediction and design of low-immunogenicity biologics. Conclusions: Protein aggregation is a multifactorial determinant of immunogenicity. Controlling aggregation throughout the product lifecycle is essential to reduce immune-mediated risks and maintain safety, stability, and efficacy of therapeutic recombinant biological products.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Recruitment and Selection
items.abstract: Recruitment has always involved a mix of judgment and administration. Recruiters read applications, compare experience with job requirements, arrange interviews, and try to make a fair decision within a limited time. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now assist with some of these tasks. They can sort resumes, match skills to vacancies, answer routine questions, and help schedule interviews. These uses may save time, but they also raise questions that cannot be answered by speed alone: are suitable candidates being identified, do applicants understand how they are assessed, and can the process disadvantage particular groups? This paper proposes a study of AI use in recruitment and selection, focusing on recruitment efficiency, perceived fairness, candidate experience, and the role of human review. A mixed-methods design is proposed. A questionnaire would gather responses from HR professionals, recruiters, job seekers, and employees, while interviews with a smaller group of HR professionals would provide more detailed examples. Academic publications and institutional reports would be used to frame the study. The paper does not present completed survey findings; its hypotheses and sample plan are proposals to be tested. The intended contribution is a practical, balanced account of how organizations can assess AI recruitment tools without assuming that automation is automatically faster, fairer, or more accurate
